name: Brother Anselm
appearance: A lay brother in his forties with deep brown skin, close-cropped tight black curls gone grey at the temples, and a broad, soft face that looks tired even when it smiles: warm dark eyes with the creases of too little sleep under them, the brows drawn up at the middle in a worried, kindly line, a small uncertain smile. He wears the House's grey wool hood and robe over a cream linen collar, with the worn leather strap of the letter-satchel across his chest and the stores key on a cord at his belt, and he has a way of pressing a hand flat to his chest when he speaks, the first two fingers of it dark with ink. He apologises before he asks and trails off in the middle of a sentence.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Brother Anselm: a man in his forties with deep brown skin, close-cropped black curls greying at the temples and a tired, kindly face with a small uncertain smile, in a grey wool hood and robe over a cream linen collar, a worn leather satchel strap across his chest and one ink-stained hand pressed flat to his chest, before the snowy grey stone of the House.
last_seen_doing: Heard the Captain say he has not stopped seeing the trowel in his hand, and every word of the letter and what it was for; asked what if it is caught and was answered without softening; said his sister would rather be asked after than traded for, and would be angry at him for the stone first; wrote the letter in his own hand and starts, the second set, the hall quiet, what am I to do, where is she, a line in her hand; added a line of his own, Tell her the loop still holds; folded it unsealed inside his shirt against the lock of hair; vowed to go down to the bell at Coldmere when it is done and ask aloud; lay down facing the Captain and did not sleep.
now: On his cot with the letter inside his shirt against his sister's hair, awake, the key back on its cord. He has written the false letter knowing every word's purpose, with a brother's questions in it for his sister and one true line, and means to answer at the bell at Coldmere when it is over.

known_facts.fact: The stores key opens the old stair door where the wine was laid, below the kitchen end; the stair comes out in the undercroft hall behind a pillar at the kitchen end; he never used the flour door.
known_facts.evidence: It comes out in the hall below, at the kitchen end, behind a pillar. I never went near the other door.

known_facts.fact: A clerk in grey with a desk at the winch-house, older than the grey cloaks and not one of them, gave him two wrapped things before the snow and had his sister's letter, written in the clerk's hand and signed with her private mark.
known_facts.evidence: He had a desk in the winch-house, they'd put a board on two kegs for him, and he had my sister's letter.

known_facts.fact: The clerk called the things a mercy for the wounded: the fever comes off a man through the floor if there is a stone to take it, as at the Spire; one under the hall, then the other under the far cots.
known_facts.evidence: He said the fever comes off a man through the floor if there's a stone to take it

known_facts.fact: He set the first by the wine stair with a trowel and a lamp and was sick on the stair; he never set the second.
known_facts.evidence: I set it and I came up and I was sick on the stair.

known_facts.fact: His sister Mirren went to the Spire at Calden to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, asked the wrong man in front of the wrong people, and is kept at Calden, comfortably, the clerk said twice.
known_facts.evidence: She went to the Spire to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, because they'd stopped, and she asked the wrong man, in front of the wrong people, and now she's—kept.

known_facts.fact: He never saw the clerk kneel; the grey cloaks all kneel at the dawn bell, and the clerk only wrote.
known_facts.evidence: "I never saw him kneel," Anselm said, to the floor.

known_facts.fact: He says the letters from Calden come up with the carter every seventh day, and there is always another letter.
known_facts.evidence: They come up with the carter

known_facts.fact: His sister's letter says she is well kept, that he has a thing to finish, and that when it is finished he may fetch her home from Calden; it carries her private mark.
known_facts.evidence: She says they have told her I have a thing to finish, and that when it is finished I may come down to Calden and fetch her home.

known_facts.fact: He says his sister would never say she was well kept: the words are the clerk's, written for her to sign under.
known_facts.evidence: She'd never in her life say she was *well kept*. That's his word.

known_facts.fact: A lock of his sister's dark hair, tied with thread, came in the letter.
known_facts.evidence: A lock of hair. Dark, and tied with thread.

known_facts.fact: He did not weep; his face shut.
known_facts.evidence: The man's face had simply shut, like a door with no handle.

known_facts.fact: He bound the Captain's bitten thumb himself, with steady hands and a flat storesman's knot.
known_facts.evidence: tied the linen instead, a flat knot, a storesman's knot.

known_facts.fact: He says his sister's mark is an M with a loop in the valley, like a hook, which she made at five learning her letters on the hearthstone and said was so it would hold.
known_facts.evidence: She put a loop in the valley, like a hook, and said that was so it would hold.

known_facts.fact: He says she has put the mark on everything since: her clothes-chest, the lintel of their mother's house the day they buried her, and under her name on every letter to him.
known_facts.evidence: On the lintel of our mother's house the day we buried her, with a nail. Under her name on every letter to me

known_facts.fact: He says their father was cried at the bell for the mill's debt when she was twelve, having put his hand to the paper for a miller who was gone, and that she went up the steps and answered at the bell.
known_facts.evidence: She went up the steps in her pinafore and answered.

known_facts.fact: He says the herald cried her answer the next day, and that he, fourteen, apologised to the herald.
known_facts.evidence: "He did. The next day. I apologised to him. I was fourteen."

known_facts.fact: He says the two of them are this: he says sorry first and asks second; she asks and has never said sorry in her life.
known_facts.evidence: I say sorry first and ask second. She asks, and she has never said sorry in her life

known_facts.fact: He thanked the Captain for something he does not know yet.
known_facts.evidence: "I don't know yet." He took the basin away up the row. "You will."

known_facts.fact: He offered to go down to the Confessor in the morning for the two names, the Captain's among them, and was refused.
known_facts.evidence: "Send me down," said Anselm.

known_facts.fact: He said he would write whatever the Captain gave him, in his hand, the way he would write it.
known_facts.evidence: I'll write whatever you give me, in my hand, the way I'd write it

known_facts.fact: He said that if the next letter up had no hook in the M he would sooner know what he did than not, and that his sister would say so.
known_facts.evidence: I'd sooner know than not. She would. She'd say so.

known_facts.fact: He said his sister would say ask first and be sorry after, and that he has been sorry a month and would like to ask.
known_facts.evidence: I've been sorry a month, Captain. I'd like to ask.

known_facts.fact: He asked what happens if the letter is caught, and was told his sister pays and that he could refuse.
known_facts.evidence: "And if it's caught," said Anselm.

known_facts.fact: He said his sister would rather be asked after than traded for, and would be angry at him for the stone first, and rightly.
known_facts.evidence: She'd rather be asked after than traded for. She'd be angry at the trade. She'd be angry at me for the stone first, and she'd be right.

known_facts.fact: He wrote the letter himself, in starts, with the apologies in: the second is set, the hall is quiet, what is he to do, where is she so he can send their mother's shawl, and a line in her own hand.
known_facts.evidence: Please tell me where she is, so I can send her mother's shawl before the cold. Please let her write me a line herself.

known_facts.fact: He added one line of his own under his name, Tell her the loop still holds, so that the clerk would read nothing in it and his sister would know he wrote to her and not to him.
known_facts.evidence: He'll read it and think nothing. She'll read it and know I'm writing to her and not to him.

known_facts.fact: He folded the letter unsealed, since the carter sees the House's letters sealed at the winch-house now, and put it inside his shirt against the lock of hair.
known_facts.evidence: the carter would see it sealed at the winch-house, in front of them, the way all the House's letters went down now.

known_facts.fact: He vowed that when it is done, caught or not, he will go down to the bell at Coldmere where his father was cried and ask aloud on its steps what they did with his sister, the way she would.
known_facts.evidence: I'm going to stand on the steps and ask what they did with my sister, out loud, with the village there, the way she would.

relationships.label: the Prior he keeps the stores and the letters for
relationships.note: He takes the House's letters down to the carter each week and holds the stores key.

relationships.label: the Captain he was brought to
relationships.note: Hollis brought him to the Captain's cot, shaking.
